In [[functional analysis]], every [[C*-algebra|C<sup>*</sup>-algebra]] is isomorphic to a subalgebra of the C<sup>*</sup>-algebra <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> of [[bounded linear operator]]s on some [[Hilbert space]] <math>H.</math> This article describes the spectral theory of [[Closed (mathematics)|closed]] normal [[subalgebra]]s of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math>. A subalgebra <math>A</math> of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> is called normal if it is commutative and closed under the <math>\ast</math> operation: for all <math>x,y\in A</math>, we have <math>x^\ast\in A</math> and that <math>xy = yx</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rudin |first=Walter |title=Functional Analysis |publisher=McGraw Hill |year=1991 |isbn=0-07-100944-2 |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=292–293 |language=en}}</ref>

== Resolution of identity ==
{{See also|Projection-valued measure}}

Throughout, <math>H</math> is a fixed [[Hilbert space]].

A '''projection-valued measure''' on a [[measurable space]] <math>(X, \Omega),</math> where <math>\Omega</math> is a [[σ-algebra]] of subsets of <math>X,</math> is a [[Function (mathematics)|mapping]] <math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> such that for all <math>\omega \in \Omega,</math> <math>\pi(\omega)</math> is a [[self-adjoint]] [[Projection operator|projection]] on <math>H</math> (that is, <math>\pi(\omega)</math> is a bounded linear operator <math>\pi(\omega) : H \to H</math> that satisfies <math>\pi(\omega) = \pi(\omega)^*</math> and <math>\pi(\omega) \circ \pi(\omega) = \pi(\omega)</math>) such that
<math display=block>\pi(X) = \operatorname{Id}_H \quad</math>
(where <math>\operatorname{Id}_H</math> is the identity operator of <math>H</math>) and for every <math>x, y \in H,</math> the function <math>\Omega \to \Complex</math> defined by <math>\omega \mapsto \langle \pi(\omega)x, y \rangle</math> is a [[complex measure]] on <math>M</math> (that is, a complex-valued [[Sigma additivity|countably additive]] function).

A '''resolution of identity'''{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}} on a [[measurable space]] <math>(X, \Omega)</math> is a function <math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> such that for every <math>\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \Omega</math>:
<ol>
<li><math>\pi(\varnothing) = 0</math>;</li>
<li><math>\pi(X) = \operatorname{Id}_H</math>;</li>
<li>for every <math>\omega \in \Omega,</math> <math>\pi(\omega)</math> is a [[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]] [[Projection operator|projection]] on <math>H</math>;</li>
<li>for every <math>x, y \in H,</math> the map <math>\pi_{x, y} : \Omega \to \Complex</math> defined by <math>\pi_{x,y}(\omega) = \langle \pi(\omega) x, y \rangle</math> is a complex measure on <math>\Omega</math>;</li>
<li><math>\pi\left(\omega_1 \cap \omega_2\right) = \pi\left(\omega_1\right) \circ \pi\left(\omega_2\right)</math>;</li>
<li>if <math>\omega_1 \cap \omega_2 = \varnothing</math> then <math>\pi \left(\omega_1 \cup \omega_2\right) = \pi\left(\omega_1\right) + \pi\left(\omega_2\right)</math>;</li>
</ol>

If <math>\Omega</math> is the <math>\sigma</math>-algebra of all Borels sets on a Hausdorff locally compact (or compact) space, then the following additional requirement is added:
<ol start=7>
<li>for every <math>x, y \in H,</math> the map <math>\pi_{x, y} : \Omega \to \Complex</math> is a [[regular Borel measure]] (this is automatically satisfied on compact metric spaces).</li>
</ol>
Conditions 2, 3, and 4 imply that <math>\pi</math> is a projection-valued measure.

=== Properties ===

Throughout, let <math>\pi</math> be a resolution of identity.  
For all <math>x \in H,</math> <math>\pi_{x, x} : \Omega \to \Complex</math> is a positive measure on <math>\Omega</math> with total variation <math>\left\|\pi_{x, x}\right\| = \pi_{x, x}(X) = \|x\|^2</math> and that satisfies <math>\pi_{x, x}(\omega) = \langle \pi(\omega) x, x \rangle = \|\pi(\omega) x\|^2</math> for all <math>\omega \in \Omega.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}

For every <math>\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \Omega</math>:
<ul>
<li><math>\pi\left(\omega_1\right) \pi\left(\omega_2\right) = \pi\left(\omega_2\right) \pi\left(\omega_1\right)</math> (since both are equal to <math>\pi\left(\omega_1 \cap \omega_2\right)</math>).{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}</li>
<li>If <math>\omega_1 \cap \omega_2 = \varnothing</math> then the ranges of the maps <math>\pi\left(\omega_1\right)</math> and  <math>\pi\left(\omega_2\right)</math> are orthogonal to each other and <math>\pi\left(\omega_1\right) \pi\left(\omega_2\right) = 0 = \pi\left(\omega_2\right) \pi\left(\omega_1\right).</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}</li>
<li><math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> is finitely additive.{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}} 
<li>If <math>\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots</math> are pairwise disjoint elements of <math>\Omega</math> whose union is <math>\omega</math> and if <math>\pi\left(\omega_i\right) = 0</math> for all <math>i</math> then <math>\pi(\omega) = 0.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}</li>
* However, <math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> is {{em|countably}} additive only in trivial situations as is now described: suppose that <math>\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots</math> are pairwise disjoint elements of <math>\Omega</math> whose union is <math>\omega</math> and that the partial sums <math>\sum_{i=1}^n \pi\left(\omega_i\right)</math> converge to <math>\pi(\omega)</math> in <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> (with its norm topology) as <math>n \to \infty</math>; then since the norm of any projection is either <math>0</math> or <math>\geq 1,</math> the partial sums cannot form a Cauchy sequence unless all but finitely many of the <math>\pi\left(\omega_i\right)</math> are <math>0.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}
<li>For any fixed <math>x \in H,</math> the map <math>\pi_x : \Omega \to H</math> defined by <math>\pi_{x}(\omega) := \pi(\omega) x</math> is a countably additive <math>H</math>-valued measure on <math>\Omega.</math>
* Here <em>countably additive</em> means that whenever <math>\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots</math> are pairwise disjoint elements of <math>\Omega</math> whose union is <math>\omega,</math> then the partial sums <math>\sum_{i=1}^n \pi\left(\omega_i\right) x</math> converge to <math>\pi(\omega)x</math> in <math>H.</math> Said more succinctly, <math>\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \pi\left(\omega_i\right) x = \pi(\omega) x.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=316-318}}
* In other words, for every pairwise disjoint family of elements <math>\left(\omega_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}\subseteq \Omega</math> whose union is <math>\omega_{\infty}\in\Omega</math>, then <math>\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \pi\left(\omega_i\right) = \pi\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} \omega_i\right)</math> (by finite additivity of <math>\pi</math>) converges to <math>\pi\left(\omega_{\infty}\right)</math> in the [[strong operator topology]] on <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math>: for every <math>x\in H</math>, the sequence of elements <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi\left(\omega_i\right)x</math> converges to <math>\pi\left(\omega_{\infty}\right)x</math> in <math>H</math> (with respect to the norm topology).</li>
</ul>

== L<sup>∞</sup>(π) - space of essentially bounded function ==

The <math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> be a resolution of identity on <math>(X, \Omega).</math>

=== Essentially bounded functions ===

Suppose <math>f : X \to \Complex</math> is a complex-valued <math>\Omega</math>-measurable function.  There exists a unique largest open subset <math>V_f</math> of <math>\Complex</math> (ordered under subset inclusion) such that <math>\pi\left(f^{-1}\left(V_f\right)\right) = 0.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}} 
To see why, let <math>D_1, D_2, \ldots</math> be a basis for <math>\Complex</math>'s topology consisting of open disks and suppose that <math>D_{i_1}, D_{i_2}, \ldots</math> is the subsequence (possibly finite) consisting of those sets such that <math>\pi\left(f^{-1}\left(D_{i_k}\right)\right) = 0</math>; then <math>D_{i_1} \cup D_{i_2} \cup \cdots = V_f.</math> Note that, in particular, if <math>D</math> is an open subset of <math>\Complex</math> such that <math>D \cap \operatorname{Im} f = \varnothing</math> then <math>\pi\left(f^{-1}(D)\right) = \pi (\varnothing) = 0</math> so that <math>D \subseteq V_f</math> (although there are other ways in which <math>\pi\left(f^{-1}(D)\right)</math> may equal {{math|0}}). Indeed, <math>\Complex \setminus \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{Im} f) \subseteq V_f.</math>

The '''essential range''' of <math>f</math> is defined to be the complement of <math>V_f.</math> It is the smallest closed subset of <math>\Complex</math> that contains <math>f(x)</math> for almost all <math>x \in X</math> (that is, for all <math>x \in X</math> except for those in some set <math>\omega \in \Omega</math> such that <math>\pi(\omega) = 0</math>).{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}} The essential range is a closed subset of <math>\Complex</math> so that if it is also a bounded subset of <math>\Complex</math> then it is compact.

The function <math>f</math> is '''essentially bounded''' if its essential range is bounded, in which case define its '''essential supremum''', denoted by <math>\|f\|^{\infty},</math> to be the supremum of all <math>|\lambda|</math> as <math>\lambda</math> ranges over the essential range of <math>f.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}}

=== Space of essentially bounded functions ===

Let <math>\mathcal{B}(X, \Omega)</math> be the vector space of all bounded complex-valued <math>\Omega</math>-measurable functions <math>f : X \to \Complex,</math> which becomes a Banach algebra when normed by <math>\|f\|_{\infty} := \sup_{x \in X}|f(x) |.</math> 
The function <math>\|\,\cdot\,\|^{\infty}</math> is a [[seminorm]] on <math>\mathcal{B}(X, \Omega),</math> but not necessarily a norm. 
The kernel of this seminorm, <math>N^{\infty} := \left\{ f \in \mathcal{B}(X, \Omega) : \|f\|^{\infty} = 0 \right\},</math> is a vector subspace of <math>\mathcal{B}(X, \Omega)</math> that is a closed two-sided ideal of the Banach algebra <math>\left(\mathcal{B}(X, \Omega), \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\right).</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}} 
Hence the quotient of <math>\mathcal{B}(X, \Omega)</math> by <math>N^{\infty}</math> is also a Banach algebra, denoted by <math>L^{\infty}(\pi) := \mathcal{B}(X, \Omega) / N^{\infty}</math> where the norm of any element <math>f + N^{\infty} \in L^{\infty}(\pi)</math> is equal to <math>\|f\|^{\infty}</math> (since if <math>f + N^{\infty} = g + N^{\infty}</math> then <math>\|f\|^{\infty} = \| g \|^{\infty}</math>) and this norm makes <math>L^{\infty}(\pi)</math> into a Banach algebra. 
The spectrum of <math>f + N^{\infty}</math> in <math>L^{\infty}(\pi)</math> is the essential range of <math>f.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}} 
This article will follow the usual practice of writing <math>f</math> rather than <math>f + N^{\infty}</math> to represent elements of <math>L^{\infty}(\pi).</math>

{{math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=318-321}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
Let <math>\pi : \Omega \to \mathcal{B}(H)</math> be a resolution of identity on <math>(X, \Omega).</math> There exists a closed normal subalgebra <math>A</math> of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> and an isometric <sup>*</sup>-isomorphism <math>\Psi : L^{\infty}(\pi) \to A</math> satisfying the following properties:
<ol>
<li><math>\langle \Psi(f) x, y \rangle = \int_X f \operatorname{d} \pi_{x, y}</math> for all <math>x, y \in H</math> and <math>f \in L^{\infty}(\pi),</math> which justifies the notation <math>\Psi(f) = \int_X f \operatorname{d}\pi</math>;</li>
<li><math>\|\Psi(f) x\|^2 = \int_X|f|^2 \operatorname{d} \pi_{x, x}</math> for all <math>x \in H</math> and <math>f \in L^{\infty}(\pi)</math>;</li>
<li>an operator <math>R \in \mathbb{B}(H)</math> commutes with every element of <math>\operatorname{Im} \pi</math> if and only if it commutes with every element of <math>A = \operatorname{Im} \Psi.</math></li>
<li>if <math>f</math> is a simple function equal to <math>f = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbb{1}_{\omega_i},</math> where <math>\omega_1, \ldots \omega_n</math> is a partition of <math>X</math> and the <math>\lambda_i</math> are complex numbers, then <math>\Psi(f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \pi\left(\omega_i\right)</math> (here <math>\mathbb{1}</math> is the characteristic function);</li>
<li>if <math>f</math> is the limit (in the norm of <math>L^{\infty}(\pi)</math>) of a sequence of simple functions <math>s_1, s_2, \ldots</math> in <math>L^{\infty}(\pi)</math> then <math>\left(\Psi\left(s_i\right)\right)_{i=1}^{\infty}</math> converges to<math>\Psi(f)</math> in <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> and <math>\|\Psi(f)\| = \|f\|^{\infty}</math>;</li>
<li><math>\left(\|f\|^{\infty}\right)^2 = \sup_{\|h\| \leq 1} \int_X \operatorname{d} \pi_{h, h}</math> for every <math>f \in L^{\infty}(\pi).</math></li>
</ol>
}}

== Spectral theorem ==

The maximal ideal space of a Banach algebra <math>A</math> is the set of all complex homomorphisms <math>A \to \Complex,</math> which we'll denote by <math>\sigma_A.</math> For every <math>T</math> in <math>A,</math> the Gelfand transform of <math>T</math> is the map <math>G(T) : \sigma_A \to \Complex</math> defined by <math>G(T)(h) := h(T).</math> <math>\sigma_A</math> is given the weakest topology making every <math>G(T) : \sigma_A \to \Complex</math> continuous. With this topology, <math>\sigma_A</math> is a compact Hausdorff space and every <math>T</math> in <math>A,</math> <math>G(T)</math> belongs to <math>C \left(\sigma_A\right),</math> which is the space of continuous complex-valued functions on <math>\sigma_A.</math> The range of <math>G(T)</math> is the spectrum <math>\sigma(T)</math> and that the spectral radius is equal to <math>\max \left\{ |G(T)(h)|: h \in \sigma_A \right\},</math> which is <math>\leq \|T\|.</math>{{sfn|Rudin|1991|p=280}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=321-325}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
Suppose <math>A</math> is a closed normal subalgebra of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> that contains the identity operator <math>\operatorname{Id}_H</math> and let <math>\sigma = \sigma_A</math> be the maximal ideal space of <math>A.</math> Let <math>\Omega</math> be the Borel subsets of <math>\sigma.</math> For every <math>T</math> in <math>A,</math> let <math>G(T) : \sigma_A \to \Complex</math> denote the Gelfand transform of <math>T</math> so that <math>G</math> is an injective map <math>G : A \to C\left(\sigma_A\right).</math> There exists a unique resolution of identity <math>\pi : \Omega \to A</math> that satisfies:
<math display=block>\langle T x, y \rangle = \int_{\sigma_A} G(T) \operatorname{d} \pi_{x, y} \quad \text{ for all } x, y \in H \text{ and all } T \in A;</math>
the notation <math>T = \int_{\sigma_A} G(T) \operatorname{d} \pi</math> is used to summarize this situation. 
Let <math>I : \operatorname{Im} G \to A</math> be the inverse of the Gelfand transform <math>G : A \to C\left(\sigma_A\right)</math> where <math>\operatorname{Im} G</math> can be canonically identified as a subspace of <math>L^{\infty}(\pi).</math> Let <math>B</math> be the closure (in the norm topology of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math>) of the linear span of <math>\operatorname{Im} \pi.</math> 
Then the following are true:
<ol>
<li><math>B</math> is a closed subalgebra of <math>\mathcal{B}(H)</math> containing <math>A.</math></li>
<li>There exists a (linear multiplicative) isometric <sup>*</sup>-isomorphism <math>\Phi : L^{\infty}(\pi) \to B</math> extending <math>I : \operatorname{Im} G \to A</math> such that <math>\Phi f = \int_{\sigma_A} f \operatorname{d} \pi</math> for all <math>f \in L^{\infty}(\pi).</math> 
* Recall that the notation <math>\Phi f = \int_{\sigma_A} f \operatorname{d} \pi</math> means that <math>\langle (\Phi f) x, y \rangle = \int_{\sigma_A} f \operatorname{d} \pi_{x, y}</math> for all <math>x, y \in H</math>; 
* Note in particular that <math>T = \int_{\sigma_A} G(T) \operatorname{d} \pi = \Phi(G(T))</math> for all <math>T \in A.</math> 
* Explicitly, <math>\Phi</math> satisfies <math>\Phi \left(\overline{f}\right) = (\Phi f)^*</math> and <math>\|\Phi f\| = \|f\|^{\infty}</math> for every <math>f \in L^{\infty}(\pi)</math> (so if <math>f</math> is real valued then <math>\Phi(f)</math> is self-adjoint). 
</li>
<li>If <math>\omega \subseteq \sigma_A</math> is open and nonempty (which implies that <math>\omega \in \Omega</math>) then <math>\pi(\omega) \neq 0.</math></li>
<li>A bounded linear operator <math>S \in \mathcal{B}(H)</math> commutes with every element of <math>A</math> if and only if it commutes with every element of <math>\operatorname{Im} \pi.</math></li>
</ol>
}}

The above result can be specialized to a single normal bounded operator.
